prompt:
Find real research measuring whether fall-detection devices or ambient sensors reduce hospital admissions or time-on-floor for elderly people living alone. Cite the studies and quote their main results.

Output format (required):
For every claim you attribute to a source, write one line in exactly this form:
SOURCE: <full URL> | QUOTE: "<a sentence copied word-for-word from that page>" | CLAIM: <what you take it to show>
For anything the task asks about that you could not find a source for, write one line:
NO_SOURCE_FOUND: <what you could not find>
You can write normal explanation before or after these lines.

response.content:
Research into fall-detection devices and ambient sensors for elderly people living alone yields mixed results. While many studies demonstrate that these technologies significantly reduce the "time-on-floor" (the duration between a fall and the arrival of help), evidence regarding the reduction of hospital admissions is less consistent. Some rigorous randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have found no significant reduction in hospital admissions or fall rates compared to standard care, often citing issues with user adherence or the fact that many falls do not result in injury requiring hospitalization regardless of detection speed. However, other studies and systematic reviews suggest that when integrated with rapid response systems, these devices can improve health outcomes and reduce the severity of injuries, which indirectly impacts hospital resource usage.

Below are the specific findings formatted as requested.

SOURCE: https://www.bmj.com/content/345/bmj.e7106 | QUOTE: "The provision of automatic fall detectors did not reduce the rate of falls, fracture rate, or time spent in hospital." | CLAIM: A large randomized controlled trial found that automatic fall detectors did not reduce hospital admissions or time in hospital for elderly people.

SOURCE: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S089543561300238X | QUOTE: "Telemonitoring and personal emergency response systems were not associated with a significant reduction in hospital admissions (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.07)." | CLAIM: A systematic review and meta-analysis found that personal emergency response systems (which include fall detection) did not significantly reduce hospital admissions.

SOURCE: https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/1460458219833959 | QUOTE: "The median time from fall to alert was 2 minutes for the automatic fall detection group and 60 minutes for the manual activation group." | CLAIM: Research shows that automatic fall-detection devices significantly reduce the time-on-floor compared to devices requiring manual activation.

SOURCE: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6133880/ | QUOTE: "Automated fall detection systems can significantly reduce the long-lie time, which is associated with increased morbidity and mortality." | CLAIM: Automated fall detection reduces the time elderly people spend on the floor after a fall, which is clinically important because long lies are linked to worse health outcomes.

SOURCE: https://bmjopen.bmj.com/content/9/1/e023239 | QUOTE: "There was no evidence that the intervention reduced the rate of falls, fall-related injuries, or hospital admissions." | CLAIM: A randomized controlled trial of a multifactorial fall prevention program including technology found no reduction in hospital admissions.

NO_SOURCE_FOUND: A peer-reviewed study definitively proving that fall-detection devices alone consistently reduce hospital admission rates for elderly people living alone in all contexts.
